pages.title: Agent skills
pages.description: Your own AI workflows as files in the vault — run them with "/" in the AI prompt or the command palette, with only the tools they declare and every change waiting for your approval.
pages.md:
A **skill** is a workflow you write once and run with `/`: "summarise what I
read this week", "sort the inbox", "check the citations in this note". It is a
folder in your vault with a `SKILL.md` file in the open
[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/specification) format, so the same file
also works in Claude Code and Codex.

## Run a skill

- In the **AI prompt**, type `/`: the skills appear under the box. Pick one,
  add what you want after its name (`/sort-inbox only this week's notes`) and
  press Enter.
- In the **command palette** (⌘K / Ctrl+K), type `/` to see the skills only.

A skill runs on the open note through Lumen's agent runtime, on your local
model first. Its answer, and every change it proposes, wait in the **review
screen**: nothing is written until you approve it.

## Starter skills

Lumen comes with six, in Hebrew:

| Skill | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/weekly-reading` — סכם את מה שקראתי השבוע | summarises the notes, clips and highlights of the last 7 days, with links |
| `/sort-inbox` — מיין את ה-inbox | proposes tags and a folder for each note in `inbox/` |
| `/book-breakdown` — פרק ספר לפרקים וכרטיסים | proposes a note per chapter, with question–answer cards |
| `/similar-notes` — מצא פתקים דומים | lists related notes, with one line on why |
| `/literature-matrix` — הכן מטריצת ספרות | proposes a table: source, question, method, findings, limits |
| `/check-citations` — בדוק ציטוטים | checks each quotation against its source note |

## Write your own

Create `.lumen/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in the vault:

```markdown
---
name: meeting-actions
description: List the action items of the open meeting note, with owners. Use after a meeting.
allowed-tools: get_document
metadata:
  title-he: משימות מהפגישה
---
1. Read the open note.
2. List every action item as "- [ ] who: what (by when)".
```

- `name`: lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, the same as the folder.
- `description`: what it does and when to use it.
- `allowed-tools`: the only tools the skill gets. Lumen's: `read_file`,
  `write_file`, `list_files`, `search_workspace`, `get_frontmatter`,
  `set_frontmatter`, `list_tags`, `get_document`, `get_selection`,
  `get_headings`, `replace_range` and the validators. Claude Code names map to
  them (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Grep`, `Glob`). A call to any other tool is
  refused. Skills never get network, Python or git tools.
- A skill in your vault with a starter's name replaces the starter.
- The first time each version of a vault skill runs, Lumen asks you, on this
  device. Only the six starters run without asking.
- Skills (like every agent) never write under dot folders (`.lumen/`, `.claude/`,
  `.git/`) or files that steer other agents (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` …).

## Skills from others

A skill that comes with a plugin, or from a vault someone shared with you (a
vault that is a git repository counts), is marked **untrusted**. The first time each version runs, Lumen shows where it
came from and which tools it asks for, and runs it only if you allow it. Its
instructions go through the injection guard, and every write or network call
it makes asks you again, on top of the review screen.

## lumen-skills: Lumen for outside agents

`packages/lumen-skills` (MIT) teaches Claude Code, Codex and other agents
Lumen's formats: `.base` views, frontmatter, niqqud, Sefaria references and
Israeli legal citation. Copy its folders into `~/.claude/skills/` (or your
agent's skills folder).

## Conformance

`npm run skills:validate` runs a port of the reference validator (`skills-ref validate`, from agentskills/agentskills) on every skill in `packages/lumen-skills`. The starter skills are checked by the tests. The name must equal the folder name, and the fields and lengths must follow the spec. A body past the spec's budget (500 lines, about 5,000 tokens) gets a warning.

A skill's instructions reach the model only when you run that skill. A list of skills offered to a model carries only names and descriptions.

pages.title: Speculative decoding in Ollama
pages.description: Ollama 0.34 speeds up some models by guessing several tokens at once. Lumen measures it per model, keeps it only where it helps, and turns it off for reproducible evals.
pages.md:
From version 0.34, Ollama turns on **speculative decoding** by default for the
models that ship a prediction head (Qwen 3.6, Qwen 3.8, Gemma 4). It
can make answers 1.3–2.4 times faster. Two catches have been reported: the
output is not always identical from run to run, even at temperature 0, and on
one model (qwen3.8) it made answers about four times *slower*.

What Lumen does:

- **Measures each model once per Ollama version.** After a model first answers,
  Lumen times a short answer in the background with Ollama's default and with
  speculation off (`draft_num_predict 0`).
- **Keeps it only where it helps.** If the default is less than 10% faster,
  Lumen turns it off for that model. So the automatic choice is never slower than off.
- **Shows the numbers** in the AI doctor (⌘K → *AI doctor*), under
  *Speculative decoding*, for example `qwen3.6:27b: 48 → 115 tok/s (×2.4, on)`.
- **Turns it off for evals.** the `eval:…` scripts (`npm run eval:agents` and the others) and `npm run models:day` send
  `draft_num_predict 0` on every request and record the Ollama version with the
  results, so a score can be reproduced.
- **Never suggests an external draft model.** A mismatched one made
  answers 73% slower in the reports.

To measure on your own machine from a terminal:

```bash
node scripts/ollama-speculative.mjs measure          # tok/s with and without, per model
node scripts/ollama-speculative.mjs repro --model qwen3.6:27b   # byte-identical with the pin?
```

pages.title: English spelling on this device
pages.description: Spell-check English notes with a dictionary that ships with Lumen — no LanguageTool account, no request leaves the device.
pages.md:
Lumen's grammar check (`⌘K → Check grammar (LanguageTool)`, and the background
underlines when *Grammar check* is on) has three backends. Which one runs
depends on the AI policy and on what you configured:

| | Under *local only* | Under *local first* / *cloud* |
|---|---|---|
| LanguageTool on this machine or network (`lumen.grammar.endpoint`, e.g. `docker/local-ai.yml` on port 8010) | used | used |
| The public LanguageTool API (`api.languagetool.org`) | **never contacted** | used |
| English dictionary on this device (this page) | used | — |
| Local proofreader model | added when you run the check yourself | — |

Hebrew paragraphs are always checked on this device (rules plus the
optional Hspell dictionary) and never sent anywhere.

## What it checks

- **Words**, against the en-US Hunspell dictionary
  ([dictionary-en](https://github.com/wooorm/dictionaries/tree/main/dictionaries/en)
  4.0, SCOWL word list, MIT AND BSD) through
  [nspell](https://github.com/wooorm/nspell) (MIT), in a background worker.
  The dictionary (≈ 0.55 MB) is part of the app: nothing is downloaded.
- **Only English paragraphs.** Each paragraph's language is detected on
  this device; a French or German paragraph is not marked as misspelled
  English. A paragraph too short to tell follows the rest of the note.
- **Only prose.** Code blocks, inline code, front matter, URLs, e-mail
  addresses, link targets, wiki links, footnote labels, `#tags`, HTML tags,
  ALL-CAPS acronyms, camelCase names and words with digits are skipped.

Hover an underline for up to three suggestions.

## Measured

On the committed dev split of the `spell-en` golden set (25 Moby-Dick
sentences with 32 injected typos), checked by
`node scripts/golden/evals/spell-en.mjs --dev` and by the unit tests:

| Metric | Result | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Typos found | 100% | ≥ 90% |
| First suggestion is the right word | 62.5% | — |
| Right word among the first five | 84.4% | — |
| Correct words marked wrong (clean sentences) | 2.6% | ≤ 3% |

Most false marks are names (*Queequeg*, *Stubb*) and British spellings
(*honour*): the dictionary is American English. The held-out test split
is scored by CI with the set's secret seed.

## Limits

- American English only; other Latin-script languages get no spelling
  check under *local only* unless you run LanguageTool yourself.
- Spelling, not grammar: "their is" passes. For grammar, run LanguageTool
  on this machine or use the explicit check, which adds the local
  proofreader model.
- There is no personal word list yet.

pages.title: Structured output and Chrome's built-in model
pages.description: How Lumen's local AI returns JSON that always matches what the feature asked for, on Ollama, the in-browser model or Chrome's built-in model — and when the built-in model is used with no download.
pages.md:
Many AI features need an answer of a fixed shape: a category, a list of tags,
a date, a task with a priority. Lumen asks every local engine for exactly that
shape (a JSON Schema) and checks every answer itself:

| Engine | How the shape is enforced |
| --- | --- |
| Ollama (desktop) | `format` with the JSON Schema |
| In-browser model (web-llm, WebGPU) | `response_format` with the schema |
| Chrome's built-in model (Chrome 148+ on desktop) | the Prompt API's `responseConstraint` |

If an answer does not match, Lumen asks once more with the error, then tries
the next engine. If an engine is not there (Firefox, Safari, a phone, no
Ollama), it is skipped without an error.

## The built-in model: AI with no download

Chrome 148 and later on Windows, macOS, Linux and Chromebook Plus can include
a small model on the device. When Chrome already has it, Lumen can use it for
**short tasks** (a category, tags, a date) without downloading anything,
which is the difference between AI in the first minute and a download screen.

- It is used only after it passed Lumen's Hebrew eval: at least 90 % of the
  score of your current local model on the same short tasks, measured on your
  Chrome version. Until then, and on every other browser, Lumen uses Ollama or
  the in-browser model.
- Lumen never starts the built-in model's download itself.
- It runs on your device: the privacy ledger lists each use as *on-device*,
  and airplane mode allows it, since nothing leaves the device.

pages.title: Grounded summaries on this device
pages.description: Summaries made on this device whose every sentence is copied from the text and checked against it — Chrome's Summarizer for English, a local model for Hebrew, and a model-free fallback.
pages.md:
`⌘K → "AI: Summarize This Note (on this device)"` and **Summarize** in the
[Ask a PDF](/workspace/pdf-chat/) panel make a short summary in which
**every sentence is copied from the text** — shortened with "…" where words
were left out — and checked against it word for word (`quoteContained`, the
rule the research citations use). A sentence that isn't in the text is
never shown. In a PDF each sentence links to its page and line.

## Layers

| Layer | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome's Summarizer API | English text, and the browser already has its model | Chrome's on-device summary — used only if at least 95 % of its sentences are in the text (it often paraphrases) |
| Local model | otherwise | the `summarizer` agent on Ollama or the in-browser model — **local executors only**, under any AI policy. For Hebrew, DictaLM 3.0 1.7B in Ollama when it is installed; else the runtime's local pick (Qwen3 in web-llm in the browser). A long text is summarised section by section, then once more over the section summaries. |
| Extractive | no local model, or nothing usable | the sentences that carry the text's most frequent content words, in their order — no model at all |

Chrome's Summarizer doesn't support Hebrew, so a Hebrew text always goes to
the local model. A model whose answer has fewer than 80 % of its sentences
in the text is asked once more, with the reason.

Install the Hebrew model in Ollama (it is listed in its library as DictaLM
3.0), and Lumen picks it for Hebrew summaries by its name.

## Measuring it

`npm run eval:summarize` summarises the documents of the golden summary set
(plan 7.10, `eval/golden/summarize`) on your Ollama and reports the share of
the model's sentences that pass the grounding check **before** any is
dropped (target: ≥ 95 %), with key-word coverage as a second signal.
`LUMEN_EVAL_SUMMARY_DIRS` adds the held-out test split built with the golden
seed, for all 20 documents.

pages.title: Reliable tool calls on small local models
pages.description: How Lumen keeps a 7–12B local model's tool calls valid. Every call is held to a JSON schema, common slips are repaired, and an invalid call gets one retry before Lumen asks you.
pages.md:
Agents use tools to do their work: they search your notes, read a file,
or propose a change. A cloud model rarely gets a tool call wrong. A small
model on your own computer, like `qwen2.5:7b` or `gemma3:12b`, often does.
Lumen does four things about it.

## 1. Every call is held to a schema

On Ollama 0.5 or later, Lumen sends a JSON schema with every turn of a
local model (Ollama's *structured outputs*). The model can only answer with
a call to one of the agent's tools, with that tool's arguments, or with
the final answer. Cloud models above the small tier still use their own
native tool calls.

## 2. Common slips are repaired

Even with a schema, small models make the same slips again and again.
Lumen fixes these before it checks the call:

- the call in a different format (`{"name", "arguments"}`, `{"function": …}`,
  `{"action", "action_input"}`)
- the arguments sent as a JSON string, or wrapped in an extra object
- the tool name in another case (`SearchNotes` for `search_notes`)
- a key in another case (`Query` for `query`)
- a number or yes/no sent as text, or one value where a list is expected
- an extra property the tool doesn't take
- trailing commas, curly quotes, and Python's `True` / `None`

Lumen never invents a value you didn't give. If something required is
missing, the call stays invalid.

## 3. One retry, then a question for you

After an invalid call, the model sees what was wrong and the tool's exact
schema, and gets one more try. If that call is invalid too, the agent stops
and asks you to say what's needed. It doesn't guess.

## 4. Nothing is written without your approval

A repaired call goes through the same checks as any other call:
permissions, the network gate, and the approval screen for changes. A
repair can't make a call do more than it was allowed to do.

## How it's measured

There are 200 requests, 100 in Hebrew and 100 in English, over ten of the
agents' tools. Each request offers five tools, and only one is right.

```sh
npm run eval:tool-calls -- --models qwen2.5:7b,gemma3:12b
```

The target is at least 95% valid calls on both models. A valid call means
the right tool with arguments that match its schema. The report also shows
how many calls the old parser would have accepted, how many were repaired
or retried, and how many ended with a question to you. The same run is one
step of `npm run models:day`.

pages.title: Translation review (the UI's seven languages)
pages.description: The agent that checks every translation of Lumen's interface against its English — missing variables, odd lengths, untranslated strings and, on this machine, a back-translation.
pages.md:
Lumen's interface is translated into seven languages (Arabic, German,
French, Hebrew, Japanese, Russian, Chinese). `npm run i18n:review` checks
every translation against its English source and prints a report:

| Check | Level | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| missing variable | error | a `{placeholder}` of the English is not in the translation — the UI would lose the value |
| extra variable | error | a `{placeholder}` the English doesn't have — it would show literally |
| length | warning | far shorter or longer than the English (Japanese and Chinese have their own bounds) |

pages.title: Local translation
pages.description: Translate a document on this device, in three layers — Chrome's built-in translator, Opus-MT for Hebrew ⇄ English, M2M100 for the rest — with code and links kept exactly.
pages.md:
`⌘K → AI: Translate Document` translates the whole note into the language
you name. Since plan 6.4 the translation runs **on this device** whenever a
local layer can take the language pair; the cloud or local LLM is the last
resort, not the first.

## The three layers

| Layer | What | Languages | Download |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · Chrome's built-in translator | Chrome's on-device Translator API | the language packs Chrome offers (Hebrew included) | a language pack, managed by Chrome, after your consent |
| 2 · Opus-MT | `opus-mt-en-he` (Apache-2.0) and `opus-mt-tc-big-he-en` (CC BY 4.0), converted to ONNX by Lumen, running in transformers.js in a worker | English ⇄ Hebrew | once, through the consent dialog below |
| 3 · M2M100 | `M2M100-418M` (MIT), same worker | about 100 languages, any pair | once, through the consent dialog |
| 3b · the AI model | the translator agent (your configured LLM) | any | — |

Which layer runs is decided by **measured quality**: each layer's chrF on the
`mt-he-en` golden set (NTREX-128, both directions) is recorded in
`src/ai/mt/quality.json`. Opus-MT is the baseline; a layer measured below
it for a pair is never chosen automatically. A layer whose quality has not
been measured yet may still run, and the toast says so ("its quality on
this pair is not measured yet").

The document's language is detected locally (plan 6.5), paragraph by
paragraph: a paragraph already in the target language is left as it is.

## Nothing downloads without asking

Before the first use of Opus-MT or M2M100 a dialog shows what the model
is for, its **size** (hundreds of MB), its **licence** and **attribution**,
and asks. A yes downloads the files once; Opus-MT's files are checked
against the checksums in `models/registry.json` and kept in this browser's
private storage (OPFS). A no leaves the document untouched and the
translation falls through to the next layer that is already available, or
to the AI model. Nothing you write is sent anywhere by the local layers.

Until the converted models are hosted (plan 15.9) layer 2 reports
"the converted models have no host yet", and the toast after a translation
lists the reason each local layer did not run.

## What never changes

Fenced and indented code, inline code, math, YAML frontmatter, every link
and image target, wiki links, autolinks, bare URLs, e-mail addresses,
footnote marks and HTML tags are kept exactly as they were. Only the words
move: headings, list items, quotes and table cells keep their markers. If a
model disturbs a protected span, the line is translated again run by run,
and the result is checked before it replaces your text.

## Measuring

```sh
node scripts/golden/evals/mt.mjs --dev --models <folder with the converted models>
```

prints chrF per layer and direction on the dev split of `mt-he-en`;
`--write-quality` records the numbers that decide the automatic choice. A
layer the harness cannot run where it is executed is reported as
"not measured", with the reason, never as a number.

## Side by side

`⌘K → Side-by-side translation` opens the current note and its translation
in two columns, one row per paragraph, so they scroll together. A Hebrew
note is translated to English; any other note to Hebrew. The note has to be
in the vault, because the translation is saved next to it as
`<note>.<lang>.md` (`notes/a.md` → `notes/a.en.md`), with a fingerprint of
each source paragraph.

When you edit a paragraph, its translation is marked **out of date**.
**Translate** sends only the paragraphs that are out of date or missing,
on the same local layers as above. Where Chrome's built-in translator is
not available (phones, other browsers), the view says so and the next
layer is used.

The translation is not written straight away. It waits in the review
panel, like every change an AI feature proposes, and it is saved to the
vault only when you approve it there.

pages.title: Voice commands, on this device
pages.description: Say "new note", "search…" or "add task…" in Hebrew or English. Lumen recognises the speech and the command locally, and asks before anything that deletes.
pages.md:
Run **Voice command** from the command palette, then say one command. Lumen
listens for one sentence (up to 8 seconds), recognises it with the
dictation model on your device, and runs the matching command. Nothing is
sent anywhere: the speech model is the one dictation already downloaded,
and the command is matched against a fixed list of phrases.

The first time, start dictation once to download the model (74 MB).

## What you can say

| Say (Hebrew / English) | What happens |
|---|---|
| ״צור פתק חדש בשם…״ / "new note called…" | A new note, with the title as its heading |
| ״חפש…״ / "search for…" | Search opens with your words in the box |
| ״הוסף משימה…״ / "add a task…" | A checkbox line in the inbox |
| ״פתח את הפתק היומי״ / "open the daily note" | Today's note |
| ״הקרא״ / "read aloud", ״הפסק להקריא״ / "stop reading" | Reads the note aloud, or stops |
| ״לכידה מהירה״ / "quick capture" | The quick-capture window |
| ״פתח משימות״ / "show my tasks" | The tasks panel |
| ״מחק את הפתק״ / "delete this note" | Asks first, then moves the note to the trash |
| ״שמור״ / "save" | Saves |
| ״סכם״ / "summarize", ״תרגם״ / "translate" | The AI summary or translation |
| ״הכתבה״ / "start dictation" | Dictation |
| ״מצב כהה״ / "dark mode" | Switches the theme |
| ״הגדרות״ / "settings", ״לוח שנה״ / "calendar", ״תצוגת גרף״ / "graph view" | Opens them |
| ״תוכן עניינים״ / "outline", ״קישורים חוזרים״ / "backlinks" | The side panels |
| ״בדוק דקדוק״ / "check grammar" | The grammar check |

You can say "please" or "um", start with "hey Lumen", and a "ו" glued to
the first word is fine. An ordinary sentence ("save the date for the
wedding") runs nothing, because a command must be the whole sentence.

## How it's measured

The phrase list was written against 200 spoken commands, 10 per command,
in Hebrew and English. It gets all 200 of them right, and runs nothing on
20 ordinary sentences. Because the list was written for those 200, that
isn't a real test. The real one is 200 commands **recorded** by different
speakers, played through the speech model:

```sh
npm run eval:voice-commands -- --script > commands.json   # the 200 sentences to read aloud
npm run eval:voice-commands -- --dir <folder with commands.json and the recordings>
```

The target is at least 90% right. The same run is a step of
`npm run models:day -- --voice-dir <folder>`.

pages.title: Hebrew Whisper on the desktop
pages.description: Transcribe long Hebrew recordings on your computer with ivrit.ai's Whisper in whisper.cpp — one sentence per line, each time a link into the audio.
pages.md:
**Command palette → 🎙 Transcribe an audio file (with timestamps).** Pick an
audio or video file. Lumen transcribes it **on this device** and inserts the
transcript at the cursor:

```md
### team-meeting.m4a

[▶ 0:00](<attachments/2026-11-10-team-meeting.m4a#t=0,6>) Good morning, everyone.
[▶ 0:06](<attachments/2026-11-10-team-meeting.m4a#t=6,14>) Today we'll go over the budget.
```

One line per sentence. Each time is a link that plays the recording from
that point. The audio is kept in `attachments/` when the workspace is
available; without one, the times are plain text.

## Which engine transcribes

| Where | Engine | When |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop app, Hebrew | ivrit.ai Whisper large-v3-turbo (ggml) in **whisper.cpp** | once it is installed (below) |
| Browser, Hebrew | ivrit.ai Whisper turbo (ONNX, WebGPU) | a GPU with f16 and enough memory |
| Anywhere | Whisper base (WASM) | otherwise, and for other languages |

Live dictation keeps the streaming Hebrew model (Zipformer): text appears
while you speak. Whisper is used for files, where accuracy matters more than
speed of the first word. For Hebrew the language is set, never guessed.

Nothing is sent anywhere. On the desktop the audio goes to a temporary file
on your computer, `whisper-cli` reads it, and the file is removed. After the
model is on disk, transcription makes no network requests.

## Setting up the desktop engine

Lumen does not bundle the model (about 1.6 GB) or the program. You install
both once:

1. **whisper.cpp** (MIT) — on macOS: `brew install whisper-cpp`, which
   provides `whisper-cli`. Lumen finds it on your `PATH`, in the app's
   `whisper` folder, or at the path in the `LUMEN_WHISPER_CLI` environment
   variable.
2. **The model file** — ivrit.ai's Hebrew Whisper large-v3-turbo as ggml
   (Apache-2.0), into the app's `whisper` folder:
   - macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/app.lumen.editor/whisper/`
   - Windows: `%APPDATA%\app.lumen.editor\whisper\`
   - Linux: `~/.local/share/app.lumen.editor/whisper/`

Lumen only uses the exact file it was built for. It checks the size and the
SHA-256 checksum before each use, and ignores any other file. If something
is missing, the command says so and uses the browser engine instead.

:::note
The model file is not pinned in this version yet: the exact Hugging Face
repository, revision and checksum still have to be filled in
(`npm run whisper:desktop -- pin` prints how). Until then the desktop engine
is not offered and files are transcribed in the browser.
:::

## Accuracy and speed (developers)

```sh
npm run whisper:desktop -- wer --split test=<folder with fleurs.json> --model <ggml file>
```

This prints WER and CER on the Hebrew test clips (FLEURS, Common Voice),
with the same normalisation as live dictation. It also prints the speed: the
real-time factor and the minutes one hour of audio takes. The targets are WER
≤ 10% on FLEURS-he test, and under 10 minutes per hour of audio on a Mac M1.

pages.title: Citations (BibTeX)
pages.description: A ```bibtex block becomes a reference list in APA 7, Chicago author-date or MLA 9 — in English or Hebrew, with nothing sent anywhere.
pages.md:
Paste BibTeX into a ` ```bibtex ` (or ` ```bib `) block and Lumen shows a
reference list. Pick the style in the block's header; the list is sorted by
author and year, with a hanging indent. Hover a reference to see its
in-text citation.

````markdown
```bibtex
% style: chicago
% lang: he
@article{watson1953molecular,
  author = {Watson, James D. and Crick, Francis H. C.},
  title = {Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid},
  journal = {Nature}, volume = {171}, number = {4356}, pages = {737--738},
  year = {1953}, doi = {10.1038/171737a0}
}
```
````

## Styles

| Style | Reference | In text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| APA 7 (default) | Watson, J. D., & Crick, F. H. C. (1953). Molecular structure of nucleic acids: A structure for deoxyribose nucleic acid. *Nature*, *171*(4356), 737–738. https://doi.org/10.1038/171737a0 | (Watson & Crick, 1953) |
| Chicago author-date (18th ed.) | Watson, James D., and Francis H. C. Crick. 1953. “Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid.” *Nature* 171 (4356): 737–38. https://doi.org/10.1038/171737a0. | (Watson and Crick 1953) |
| MLA 9 | Watson, James D., and Francis H. C. Crick. “Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid.” *Nature*, vol. 171, no. 4356, 1953, pp. 737–38, https://doi.org/10.1038/171737a0. | (Watson and Crick) |

- **APA** turns the title into sentence case. Words in braces keep their
  capitals (`{DNA}`, `{Wonderland}`), as do acronyms and the first word
  after a colon. A German title (`langid = {german}`) keeps its capitals.
- **Chicago** and **MLA** keep the title as written and shorten page ranges
  by their rules (737–38). MLA drops *Company* / *Co.* from publishers and
  writes *University Press* as *UP*.

## Hebrew

`% lang: he` (or Hebrew as the interface language) changes the words, not
the order: *and* / *&* → ו (ו- before a Latin name), *et al.* → ואחרים,
MLA's *vol.* / *no.* / *pp.* → כרך / גיליון / עמ׳. Names, titles and
publishers stay as published. Each reference keeps its own direction.

## Offline

Formatting is Lumen's own rules (no citeproc, no CSL files, no download).
Whether citeproc can be used is an open licensing decision (plan 15.10);
the rules here are the fallback the plan names. Looking up a DOI is not
part of the block — it stays offline.

pages.title: Math inside Hebrew text
pages.description: Formulas in a right-to-left sentence keep their order in the editor, the preview, PDF and Word.
pages.md:
A formula in the middle of a Hebrew sentence breaks in almost every editor.
`x² + y² = r²` comes out as `r² = y² + x²`, or the `$` signs jump to the
other end. In Lumen a formula is laid out **left to right as one unit**,
wherever it sits in a right-to-left line:

```markdown
במדגם של 40 תלמידים קיבלנו $\bar{x}=12.5$ וזה נכון ב-95% מהמקרים.
```

## Where it holds

- **Preview and print (PDF).** Each formula is an isolated left-to-right
  block, so its pieces (`a =`, `b +`, `c`) stay in order. Formulas are drawn
  by Temml as MathML, which the browser typesets itself, when the app has
  Temml. Otherwise KaTeX draws them. Either one loads only when a note has
  math.
- **Source editor.** `$…$` is an isolated left-to-right run. The digits,
  operators and `$` signs stay where you typed them, and the cursor moves
  through the formula the way it is drawn.
- **WYSIWYG.** An inline formula is an isolated left-to-right run.
- **Line direction.** A formula does not decide a line's direction. A Hebrew
  sentence that opens with a formula, such as `$x^2$ הוא ריבוע`, is still
  right to left. `$$` display blocks are always left to right, like code.
- **Word (.docx).** Each formula becomes a Word math zone, which Word lays out
  left to right as one unit inside the Hebrew paragraph. The zone holds the
  TeX as written; Lumen does not convert it to Word's built-up equations.

## Typing formulas

- **Ctrl+M** (**⌘M** on a Mac) wraps the selection in `$…$`, or inserts `$$`
  with the cursor between. It also works with the Hebrew layout on. The
  command palette has **Insert inline formula** too.
- **No layout switch inside a formula.** With the Hebrew layout on, keys
  typed inside `$…$` in the source editor come out as the Latin letter of
  the same key: the X key types `x`, not `ס`. Outside the formula, typing is
  unchanged.

## Templates

The template gallery has three study templates, in English and Hebrew:

- **Math exam practice** (בגרות): a quadratic equation, a derivative, sequences;
- **Physics lab report**: theory, a measurement table, error analysis;
- **Statistics problem set**: descriptive statistics, a z-score, a hypothesis
  test.

## Limits

- **What counts as a formula.** A `$` followed by a space, or a closing `$`
  followed by a digit, does not open or close one. So `$5 ו-$10` is money.
  This follows Pandoc's rule, which can differ from the preview's Markdown
  parser in rare cases.
- **Typing with the Hebrew layout** works in the source editor. In WYSIWYG,
  the formula editor does not translate keys.

pages.title: Dynamic blocks reference
pages.description: The fenced code-block languages that Lumen renders as live, interactive previews.
pages.md:
Lumen's killer feature is **dynamic blocks**: write a fenced code block in markdown, and the preview renders it as a chart, diagram, table, map, or live sandbox. Every block degrades gracefully — if rendering fails, you still see the source.

## Quick-reference table

| Fence | Renders as | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ` ```mermaid ` | Inline SVG diagram (flowcharts, sequence, gantt, class, state, ER) | Mermaid v11; lazy-loaded |
| ` ```chart ` | ECharts (line / bar / pie / scatter / heatmap / radar / boxplot / treemap / sunburst / sankey) | YAML or JSON spec |
| ` ```csv ` / ` ```tsv ` | Sortable / filterable DataTable + auto-chart suggestion | Title via `title="..."` |
| ` ```sheet ` | A small spreadsheet: CSV cells, and `=` formulas with A1 references and ranges | See [Sheet block](/blocks/sheet/) |
| ` ```json-table ` | DataTable from a JSON array | Array of objects required |
| ` ```sql ` / ` ```pandas ` / ` ```object ` / ` ```data ` | Tabular display via the shared `DataBlock` renderer | `pandas` parses DataFrame `to_dict()` shape |
| ` ```map ` / ` ```geojson ` | Leaflet map (tile, markers, polygons, popups) | GeoJSON or YAML map-spec |
| ` ```dot ` / ` ```graphviz ` | Graphviz diagram via WASM | Rendered locally — no Kroki dependency |
| ` ```plantuml ` / ` ```puml ` | PlantUML via kroki.io | Network egress; opt out via privacy mode |
| ` ```abc ` | ABC music notation (renderable score) | Abcjs |
| ` ```model ` | 3-D model viewer (`<model-viewer>`) | GLB / GLTF |
| ` ```embed ` | Universal embed (YouTube, Vimeo, Twitter, Loom, CodePen, Spotify, Gist, …) | URL on the body line. Nothing loads until you click **Load** (or **Always allow** the site): then the player runs inside Lumen's content frame. A link to a site Lumen can't embed stays a link |
| ` ```html ` / ` ```html-preview ` | Sanitized HTML preview | DOMPurify allowlist; no JS executes in the page |
| ` ```svg ` / ` ```live-svg ` | Sanitized inline SVG preview | Same hardening as HTML |
| ` ```live-js ` | JS sandbox (Worker isolate) with console output | Stdout/stderr/error states; timeout-protected; `shared` = one REPL scope per document (see below) |
| ` ```live-lua ` / ` ```lua-live ` | Lua 5.4 (wasmoon WASM) in a Web Worker, with `print`/`io.write` output and return values | Loads on Run; self-hosted wasm (no CDN); `timeout=` ms (default 5000) |
| ` ```live-r ` / ` ```r-live ` | R (webR, WebAssembly): printed output, messages, warnings, errors and base-graphics plots | webR is GPL-3.0, so Lumen doesn't ship it: the first Run on a device offers the download (~45 MB from webr.r-wasm.org, licence shown first, every file checked against the build's checksums), then it stays on the device and works offline; `timeout=` ms (default 30000); base R + bundled recommended packages, no CRAN installs |
| ` ```live-ruby ` / ` ```ruby-live ` | Ruby 3.4 (ruby.wasm) in a sandboxed Web Worker: `puts`/`warn` output, the last value (`=> …`), errors with `block:<line>` | Loads on first Run (~30 MB, self-hosted, cached); `timeout=` ms (default 10000; a runaway loop is killed); full stdlib (`require "json"`, `set`, …), no gems; fresh VM per run; no network, storage or JS bridge |
| ` ```playground [react\|vue] ` / ` ```web-playground ` | A small multi-file web project run live: files separated by `--- name.ext ---` lines (HTML, CSS, JS, JSX, TS, JSON); Preview, a tab per file, and a Console | Runs in a sandboxed iframe on its own origin (no access to your documents); JSX / TypeScript via Sucrase; `react` / `react-dom` (18) and `vue` (3, with the template compiler) are provided offline — other packages aren't; entry is `main.*`; `height=` px |
| ` ```live-css ` | Sandboxed iframe HTML+CSS preview | `srcdoc` + sandbox flags |
| ` ```live-glsl ` / ` ```glsl ` / ` ```shader ` | GLSL fragment shader on a quad | Hot-reloads on edit |
| ` ```bibtex ` / ` ```bib ` | Citation list (formatted from BibTeX) | Click → copy citation |
| ` ```database ` | Workspace-wide database query (markdown frontmatter as the "table") | Lumen-native query DSL |
| ` ```insights ` / ` ```jsonl ` | JSONL analyzer: conclusions, freq, charts, file generators | No external model |
| ` ```code-doctor ` / ` ```fix-json ` | Malformed JSON/JSONL repair with diff + accept-fix UI | 7-pass tolerant tokenizer |

## Live JavaScript — shared scope (REPL across blocks)

By default every ` ```live-js ` block runs in its own fresh Web Worker, so nothing one block defines is visible to another. Add `shared` to the fence to turn the blocks of a document into one REPL session:

````markdown
```live-js shared
const prices = [12, 7, 30]
function total(xs) { return xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) }
```

Some prose in between…

```live-js shared
console.log(total(prices))   // 49
```
````

- All `shared` blocks of the open document use **one worker**, and its global scope persists across runs and across blocks. Top-level `const` / `let` / `var`, `function` and `class` declarations become globals of that worker, so later runs and later blocks can use them. Declarations nested in blocks, functions or loop heads stay local.
- As in a browser console, running a block again may redeclare its names, and top-level `const` bindings can be reassigned by later runs.
- Blocks share state in the order they **run**. Each block runs when it renders and when you click **Run**; runs are queued and execute one at a time.
- `shared=name` (for example ` ```live-js shared=physics `) gives a separate named scope inside the same document. Different documents never share a scope.
- **Reset scope** (shown on shared blocks) discards the worker and every global in it; the next run starts fresh. Re-run the blocks you depend on afterwards.
- Sandboxing is unchanged: the worker has no DOM and no access to the page, shared mode adds no module or network-import support (the page CSP still applies inside the worker), and a run that exceeds the 8-second timeout is stopped. A timeout terminates the worker, which also resets the scope.
- An unused scope is disposed five minutes after the last shared block of that document unmounts.

## Live Lua

````markdown
```live-lua height=200 timeout=3000
local function fib(n) return n < 2 and n or fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) end
for i = 1, 10 do io.write(fib(i), " ") end
print()
return _VERSION
```
````

Click **Run** to execute. Nothing is downloaded until then; the ~270 KB `glue.wasm` is bundled with Lumen and served from the same origin, so it works offline and under the app's CSP. Each run gets a fresh Web Worker and a fresh Lua state:

- `print` and `io.write` stream to the output panel; values `return`ed from the chunk are shown after a `→`.
- Errors show the line (`block:2: boom`).
- A runaway loop is stopped after `timeout` ms (100–60000, default 5000) by an instruction-count hook, and the page kills the worker if it stops responding. **Stop** cancels a run.
- The Lua heap is capped at 64 MB and captured output at 200 000 characters.
- The standard libraries are available except process and file access: `os.exit`, `os.execute`, `os.getenv`, `os.remove`, `os.rename`, `io.open`, `io.popen`, `io.read`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile` and `package` are removed. Lua cannot reach JavaScript objects.

## Security & hardening

All HTML, SVG, and embed renderers funnel through `src/lib/markupSanitizer.ts`. The sanitizer:

- Strips every `on*` attribute via a prefix-matching hook (not just the named list, so future handlers like `onpointerdown` are caught).
- Blocks `style` attributes containing `expression(...)`, `url(javascript:...)`, or `behavior:`.
- Allows only image-MIME `data:` URIs (everything else, including `data:text/html`, is dropped).
- Rejects `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, and unknown protocols.

Each dynamic block is wrapped in an `ErrorBoundary` so a single broken block doesn't take down the whole preview.

## Lazy loading

Every block is `React.lazy`-imported. A block's library (Mermaid, ECharts, Leaflet, …) loads only when a note that uses it is opened, so adding block types never grows the startup bundle. That bundle has a size budget, checked on every pull request (`scripts/bundle-budget.mjs`).

## Authoring a new block

See [Plugin SDK](/plugins/sdk/) — every block is a React component registered with `registerPlugin`. The `pluginSystem` wires its fence language to a tag, mounts via `Suspense`, and routes it through the renderer pipeline.

## Web Playground

````markdown
```playground react height=260
--- App.jsx ---

export default function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>Clicked {n} times</button>;
}
--- main.jsx ---


createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render();
--- style.css ---
button { font: 16px system-ui; }
```
````

- **Files:** `--- name.ext ---` starts a file. A body without markers is one file (`main.jsx` for React, `main.js` otherwise). `index.html` is the page body (default `<div id="root">`, or `<div id="app">` for Vue); its `<script>` tags don't run, so put code in files.
- **Imports:** relative imports between files (with or without the extension), CSS / JSON files, and the provided `react`, `react-dom`, `react-dom/client`, `react/jsx-runtime` and `vue`.
- **Isolation:** each Run loads a fresh runner document in a sandboxed iframe with an opaque origin and its own Content-Security-Policy. The project can't read the app's storage, cookies or page.

pages.title: Sheet block
pages.description: A small spreadsheet inside a note, stored as CSV, with A1 formulas on the app's formula engine.
pages.md:
A ` ```sheet ` block is a small spreadsheet. Its content is CSV, so the note
stays plain Markdown and Obsidian shows it as a code block. A cell that
starts with `=` is a formula.

````markdown
```sheet
מוצר,מחיר,כמות,סה״כ
תפוחים,4.5,3,=B2*C2
"שוקולד, מריר",12,2,=B3*C3
,,,=SUM(D2:D3)
```
````

- **References:** `B3`, `$B$3` (the `$` is accepted), and ranges such as
  `A1:A5` or `A1:C4`.
- **Functions:** the database formula functions, written in any case:
  `SUM`, `AVERAGE`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT`, `IF`, `ROUND`, `ABS`, `LEN`,
  `UPPER`, `&` to join text, and the rest of
  [formulas](/workspace/database-formulas/).
- **Commas:** a comma inside a formula's parentheses belongs to the formula,
  so `=IF(A1>5, "high", "low")` needs no CSV quotes.
- **Right to left:** a Hebrew sheet runs right to left, with column A on the
  right as in Hebrew Excel. The arrow keys move the way they point on
  screen; Home and End go to the row's ends. The bar above the grid shows
  the focused cell's formula.
- **Errors:** a circular reference shows `#CYCLE!` in every cell on the
  cycle, and the bar names the path (`A1 → B1 → A1`). A formula that fails
  shows `#ERROR!`, and a range of more than 10,000 cells shows `#RANGE!`.

To change a cell, edit the CSV in the source view.

pages.title: Encrypted live sharing
pages.description: Share a note live through a server that stores and relays only ciphertext, names and cursors included.
pages.md:
A note you share from Lumen goes through the collab server end-to-end
encrypted. The server keeps people to their [roles](/collab/sharing/) and
holds the room's history, but it can't read the note, its comments, or
who is in it and where their cursor is.

## What the server sees

| | Encrypted in the browser | What the server holds |
|---|---|---|
| The note | Yes (AES-GCM-256, a [ciphertext transport document](/collab/encryption/)) | Envelopes `{v, iv, ct}` |
| Comment threads | Yes, the same way (`<room>~comments`) | Envelopes |
| Presence: names, colours, cursors | Yes (since plan W2.20) | `{ "e2e": "<base64>" }` per participant |
| The room key | It never leaves the link | Nothing |
| Room name, share ids, roles, expiry | No (the server needs them) | Those, in SQLite |

The room key is in the link's fragment, after the `#`
(`#room=…&password=…&share=…`). Browsers never send the fragment to a
server, and Lumen never puts the key in a request: token requests carry
the room name, the share id or owner secret, and the operator's access key.

## Sealed rooms

An encrypted client asks for its token with `e2ee: true`, and the server
**seals** the room. From then on, for good:

- an update that writes anything except ciphertext envelopes (text, a map
  entry, a nested type, an array element that isn't an envelope) is
  refused and its connection dropped, before it reaches the room;
- a presence state with any field except `e2e` is refused the same way;
- a document that isn't ciphertext-only is never written to disk.

A room that already stores readable content (an old plaintext room) is not
sealed. To run a server that takes encrypted rooms only, set
`COLLAB_REQUIRE_E2EE=1`: every room is then sealed and plaintext clients
can't write at all.

The server checks the shape. It can't tell ciphertext from other bytes
inside `ct`; what keeps `ct` unreadable is the client, which only ever
writes AES-GCM output there.

## Encrypted presence

Each participant has two awareness instances. The editor's cursors and the
peer list use the plain one, which no provider touches. The providers sync
a transport awareness where each state is the plain state sealed under the
room key. Two values are bound into the seal:

- the participant's client id (in the GCM tag), so a relay can't show one
  participant's name or cursor as someone else's;
- a counter that only goes up, so a relay can't replay an older cursor.

A state that isn't sealed, or doesn't open with the room key, is never shown.

## Sharing needs an encrypted room

The share dialog makes links only for a room with its own key, which every
new collaboration session has. For a session joined from an old link
without a key, start a new session first.

## How it's checked

`src/__tests__/collabE2eeSharing.test.ts` runs the real server and records
every WebSocket frame both ways:

- the note's text (Hebrew and English), a comment, both participants'
  names, a cursor and the room key: **0 hits** in the traffic, the stored
  states and every file in the server's data directory. The same search on
  a room that isn't encrypted does find the text, so the check can fail;
- a plaintext writer, and plaintext presence, are refused in a sealed room;
- an edit reaches the other participant in under 150 ms (p95 over 40 edits);
- a 1 MB note with 5 participants and 1,000 random edits converges with 0
  edits lost, and a sixth participant gets the same note from the server.

## Limits

- The server still sees metadata: the room name, how many people are
  connected, when they edit and how much.
- Anyone with the link has the key. Revoking a link cuts its holder off
  from the server within seconds, but a copy of the note they already have
  stays theirs.

pages.title: End-to-end encryption for collab
pages.description: Add a room password and no relay, signaling server or sync server can read your document.
pages.md:
Lumen's WebRTC mesh is unencrypted by default: peers sync the Yjs
document directly, so a signaling server that relays messages, a
persistent collab server (Hocuspocus), or anyone who joins with the room
link can read the content. Setting a **room password** switches the
room to an end-to-end encrypted transport. Document content is then
only ever readable by peers that know the password.

## Turn it on

```js
// Either:
localStorage.setItem("lumen.collab.password", "open-sesame-12345");

// Or append to the share link:
//   #room=lumen-bright-river-77&password=open-sesame-12345
```

Every peer in the room must use the same password. A peer with the
wrong password can still connect, but it only receives ciphertext it
can't decrypt. Nothing is applied to its document, and it sees a
"Can't decrypt this room" error.

> Putting the password in the URL hash keeps it out of HTTP requests
> (browsers never send the `#fragment`), but it still lands in browser
> history and anywhere you paste the link. For anything sensitive,
> share the room link and the password through different channels.

## How it works

Each peer keeps **two** Yjs documents:

| Document | Contents | Attached to the network? |
|---|---|---|
| Plaintext doc | Text, comments, everything the editor shows | **No.** It stays in the tab. |
| Transport doc | One append-only `Y.Array` of ciphertext envelopes | Yes (y-webrtc, and the persistent server if configured) |

1. **Key derivation:** PBKDF2-SHA-256, 200 000 iterations, salt
   `lumen.collab.v2|<room name>`. The same password in two different
   rooms gives two unrelated keys.
2. **Outbound:** each local edit to the plaintext doc produces a Yjs
   update. Edits made in the same tick are merged into one update,
   encrypted with AES-GCM-256 under a fresh random 12-byte IV, and
   appended to the transport array as `{ v: 2, iv, ct }`. The format
   version and the snapshot flag are bound into the GCM tag as
   additional authenticated data.
3. **Inbound:** each envelope that appears in the transport array (from
   a peer or from the persistence server) is decrypted and applied to
   the plaintext doc with origin `e2e-remote`. The outbound listener
   ignores that origin, so received edits are never encrypted again
   (no update loop). If decryption fails, the envelope is dropped and
   the user sees an error. Unauthenticated bytes are never applied.
4. **Late joiners:** a peer that joins later receives the whole
   transport array through the normal Yjs sync, decrypts every envelope
   and rebuilds the document. Yjs buffers updates that arrive before
   their dependencies, so envelopes can be decrypted in any order.
5. **Compaction:** when the array grows past 500 envelopes, the peer
   that just wrote one encrypts a full-state snapshot (`s: 1`) and
   deletes only the envelopes it has already applied. A peer that has
   ever failed to decrypt something never compacts, so it can't throw
   away history it couldn't read.

## Who can read what

| Party | Document text & comments | Room name | Envelope count, sizes, timing | Presence: names, colours, cursor anchors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peer with the password | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Peer without the password | **No** | Yes | Only through a persistence server it can reach | **No** — it can't complete the WebRTC handshake |
| Signaling server | **No** | Yes | Traffic shape only (its messages are encrypted with the password) | **No** |
| persistent collab server (Hocuspocus) | **No** (it stores only ciphertext) | Yes | Yes | **No** — Lumen publishes no presence to it |
| Network eavesdropper | No (WebRTC is DTLS-encrypted anyway) | Depends on the signaling transport | Traffic shape | No |

### Persistent rooms store only ciphertext

With [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/) the persistent server
syncs the **transport** doc. Its database holds the envelope array and
never a key, so a leaked server backup reveals no document content. A
peer that joins later still needs the password to read the history.

## Limits: what this does *not* protect

- **Awareness / presence reaches every peer that holds the password.**
  The room password is also given to y-webrtc, which encrypts all
  signaling and BroadcastChannel traffic with a key derived from it, and
  peer connections are DTLS-encrypted — so the signaling server and peers
  *without* the password never see display names, colours or cursors.
  Presence itself is not wrapped in Lumen's envelopes, though: every
  password holder sees it. Cursor positions are Yjs *relative positions*
  (item IDs: client id + clock, no document text). The persistent
  persistent server receives no presence from Lumen.
- **Metadata:** room name, number of peers, number and size of
  envelopes, and when they are written. Size and timing can hint at
  how much is being typed.
- **Integrity of the history as a whole.** Each envelope is
  authenticated, but a malicious relay or persistence server can
  *drop* or *withhold* envelopes, or delete them from the array. That
  makes peers diverge or lose edits, but it can never inject or alter
  content. Replayed envelopes are harmless because Yjs updates are
  idempotent.
- **Anyone with the password.** All peers who know it are trusted
  equally. A peer with the password can also delete envelopes from the
  shared array.
- **Weak passwords.** The key comes only from the password and the room
  name, both of which a server operator knows. An attacker holding the
  ciphertext can run an offline guessing attack, slowed by 200 000
  PBKDF2 iterations per guess. Use a long passphrase.
- **No forward secrecy, no key rotation inside a room.** A password
  that leaks later decrypts all stored history. To rotate, create a
  new room with a new password (see below).
- **Local storage.** Version-history snapshots and saved files on each
  peer are plaintext on that device. Use a Vault password
  (`⌘K → Encrypt document`) for at-rest encryption.

## Rotating

The key is tied to the room, so the clean way to rotate is to move to
a new room with a new password:

```js
localStorage.setItem("lumen.collab.password", "new-stronger-passphrase");
```

Then leave and start a fresh room, seeding it from your current
document. If you change the password while staying in the same room,
peers on the old password get "Can't decrypt" errors, and the old
history stays encrypted under the old key on any persistence server.

## Trade-offs

- A misplaced password locks everyone out. Treat it like any shared
  secret and share it through a side channel (Signal, 1Password, etc.).
- The PBKDF2 derivation runs once per password and room. That is about
  100 ms on modern devices, but noticeable on old phones.
- Each edit batch adds about 40 bytes of overhead (IV + GCM tag +
  envelope framing). Long sessions grow the array until compaction
  kicks in at 500 envelopes.

pages.title: Havruta: study with a partner
pages.description: A shared, end-to-end encrypted study room on a Sefaria reference. Your notes travel, the text stays on each device, and the room is deleted when you finish.
pages.md:
A havruta room is a study session for two on one reference, such as a daf, a
chapter or a verse. Each of you sees the text with its translation where its
licence allows, and next to every segment your notes and your partner's.

## Start a session

1. Put the cursor on a reference in a note, for example `Berakhot 2a` or
   `בראשית א:א`, or open the reference's saved source note.
2. In the command palette, choose **Study with a partner (havruta)…**.
3. Send your partner the invite: **Copy invite link**, or **Invite QR code**
   to show on screen. No account is needed.

## What travels and what doesn't

- **The text never leaves your device.** The room holds the reference, your
  notes, highlights (as positions, not words) and where each of you is. Each
  side loads the text itself: from the vault's offline copy first, otherwise
  from Sefaria after you agree, as when you insert a source.
- A note that repeats six or more words of the text in a row is refused.
  Point at the segment instead. This keeps the room clear of texts whose
  licence does not allow sharing.
- A version whose licence does not allow copying is never loaded. It is
  listed with its licence and a link to read it on Sefaria.
- Everything in the room is end-to-end encrypted with the room's password,
  which is only in the invite link's `#` part. The relay sees ciphertext.

## On the study screen

- **↑ / ↓, Home / End** move between segments; **Enter** goes to the note
  box and **Escape** comes back.
- **Follow my partner** scrolls with your partner. Their place and their
  selection show in their colour.
- **Hide niqqud / Show niqqud** changes only what you see. Unpointed text,
  such as Aramaic, can be pointed on the device for reading.

## Offline, and the end of a session

- A session works without a network: your notes are kept on the device and
  merge with your partner's when you both reconnect.
- **Save to vault** writes a note named `חברותא — <reference> — <date>` in
  `Havruta/`, with both partners' notes and a link to the passage.
- **End session** saves that note and deletes the room from the relay. Your
  partner's screen saves its own note too. A room nobody touches for 30 days
  is deleted anyway.

pages.title: Live canvas
pages.description: Draw on one canvas together during a collab session — edits and pointers appear as they happen, over the same encrypted room as the note.
pages.md:
When you share a note in a live session, the canvas you open is shared too.
Everyone in the room who opens the same canvas (same name) sees the others'
shapes, text and arrows change as they draw, and their pointers with their
names.

## How it works

- The canvas travels in the session's document, next to the note. In a room
  with a password it is end-to-end encrypted like the note. On the public
  server, the room only lets in people who hold the share link's password
  ([persistent rooms](/collab/persistent/)). Nothing about the drawing
  reaches a server in the clear.
- Two people can change the same shape at the same moment. Lumen uses
  Excalidraw's own rule: every change of a shape has a version number, and
  the later one wins. On a tie, every copy picks the same one. All copies end
  on the same drawing, in whatever order the changes arrive.
- What you are dragging, resizing or typing in stays as you have it until
  you let go.
- A change made by someone else doesn't go into your undo history: ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z
  undoes only your own changes.
- A deleted shape is deleted for everyone.

Each person's copy is still saved to their own vault
(`canvases/<name>.excalidraw`). JSON Canvas export and the note cards work as
on a canvas of your own.

## Limits

- Images added to a live canvas are not sent to the others yet. They see the
  frame where the image is.
- The target is 5,000 shapes at 60 frames per second, and a change seen by
  the others within 150 ms (95th percentile). The nightly run measures the
  frame rate on a real computer. The tests measure the delay over a simulated
  relay.

pages.title: Persistent rooms
pages.description: Keep a collaboration room alive when every peer has left, with a small y-websocket server you run yourself.
pages.md:
A plain [WebRTC room](/collab/webrtc/) lives only in the browsers that are
in it: when the last person leaves, the room is gone (whoever saved the
note keeps their copy). A **persistent server** keeps each room's
document, so anyone can join later and find the latest version, even when
nobody else is online.

## Run the server

`sync-server/persistent-server.js` is a small
[y-websocket](https://github.com/yjs/y-websocket) server that stores every
room on disk with LevelDB.

```bash
cd sync-server
npm install @y/websocket-server y-leveldb
PORT=4444 node persistent-server.js        # ws://localhost:4444
```

- **Storage:** `YJS_STORAGE_DIR` (default `./.yjs-persistence`). On Fly.io,
  Render or Railway, point it at a mounted volume. The Docker compose
  bundle uses `/data/yjs`.
- **Access token:** start it with `COLLAB_TOKEN=<a long random string>`
  and it accepts only clients that send the same token. Without one,
  anyone who knows a room name can read the room's (encrypted) updates
  and add their own.
- **Health:** `GET /healthz` answers `200 {"ok":true}`.
- Put it behind TLS (`wss://`) before you expose it.

`DEPLOY.md` has the Fly.io steps.

## Point Lumen at it

Set it when you build Lumen:

```bash
VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_URL=wss://collab.example.com
VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN=<the same COLLAB_TOKEN>   # if the server has one
```

Lumen then connects to the server alongside the peer-to-peer mesh. Where
billing is configured, persistent rooms need a Pro or Team plan; a
self-hosted build without billing has them on.

## What the server can read

Nothing, in a room with a password. The server stores only the
AES-GCM-256 ciphertext envelopes, never the text. Rooms created today
have 128-bit random names and are end-to-end encrypted, so the token is
a second gate, not the only one. What the server does see: room names,
and the size and timing of updates. See
[End-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/#persistent-rooms-store-only-ciphertext).

pages.title: The public server
pages.description: A free live-share server for everyone that stores only encrypted rooms, deletes idle rooms after 90 days and keeps no IP addresses in its logs.
pages.md:
Live sharing works without any server: browsers connect to each other
directly over [WebRTC](/collab/webrtc/). A server adds two things. People on
different networks find each other (signaling), and a room stays available
when nobody else is online ([persistent rooms](/collab/persistent/)).

Lumen's public server does both, free, and **never sees what you write**.

## What the server can and can't see

| | The server |
|---|---|
| The text of your note | **Never.** It accepts only rooms with a password ([end-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/)). Every change is checked before it is applied. A change that is not an encrypted envelope closes the connection, and nothing of it is stored. |
| The room's encrypted document | Stored, so a room survives everyone leaving. It is ciphertext. Without the room password nobody can read it, the server included. |
| Who may join a room | Only someone with the room password. The app proves it holds the password with a value derived from it, which is not the encryption key. The server keeps only a hash of that value. The room's name on the server carries a commitment to that hash, so the room accepts only the value that matches it, even from the first person to connect. Knowing a room's name is not enough to join it, write to it, keep it or lock its owners out. A new room also costs the app a few seconds of work. |
| How many new rooms | Limited per day: 2,000 on the whole server, 20 per address (an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 /64) and 80 per IPv6 /48. What is stored is limited too: 20,000 rooms, 4 GB in all, and 50 rooms and 20 MB per address and per IPv6 /48. When the server is full, a new room takes the place of stored rooms that nobody else joined again in the last 14 days and nobody is connected to: the smallest one that frees one room's share of the space, or else a few smaller ones that free it together. Your own return doesn't count (from the same address, or from the same IPv6 /48); a return from another address does. The rooms of an address or /48 that has grown past its 20 MB go first, even if someone came back to them. What you write in someone else's room counts toward your 20 MB, not theirs. A request that can't get a room removes none (it still counts toward that address's 20 a day). Addresses are counted under a keyed hash that changes every day, never stored as such; a stored room keeps only a 20-bit hash of the address that made it, which about 4,000 IPv4 addresses share. Past a limit, a new room works peer to peer only, and rooms that already exist are not affected. |
| Rooms nobody uses | Deleted **90 days** after the last change. Only a change counts, and only someone with the room password can make one: connecting, or only reading, stores nothing. |
| Study rooms (havruta) | Deleted **30 days** after the last change, or right away when someone presses **End session**. Only someone with the room password can delete a room: the request carries the value derived from the password that the room's name commits to. The text you study is never in the room, only your notes and highlights, encrypted. |
| Your IP address | Not in any log. The server code logs nothing about connections, and request logging is off. Cloudflare, which hosts the server, sees addresses as any network provider does. |
| Cursors and display names | Passed between the people in the room while they are connected. Never stored. The name is a random one ("Saffron", "Willow"), not yours. |
| Room names, times and sizes | Visible to the server. Room names are random. |

## If the server is down

The app keeps working. Rooms connect peer to peer over WebRTC, and your
notes are on your device. The server's health is at `/healthz` for uptime
monitors.

## Where it runs and why

On **Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects**, on the free plan: one small
object per room, created near the first person who opens it (Cloudflare has
a data center in Tel Aviv). We compared three free options:

- **Cloudflare Workers + Durable Objects** (chosen): free plan includes
  WebSockets with hibernation, SQLite storage (5 GB) and 100,000 requests a
  day; 100 WebSocket messages count as 5 requests.
- **Fly.io**: no longer has a free allowance for new accounts.
- **Deno Deploy**: WebSockets work, but there is no single place that holds
  a room, so peers on different instances would not see each other.

## Running it

The server is `edge-workers/collab/` (it uses the same room code as the
Node server in `sync-server/`). Whoever owns the Cloudflare account deploys
it with one command:

```sh
npm run collab:deploy
```

It deploys the Worker, sets the token secret, checks `/healthz` and prints
the two build variables for the app: `VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_URL` and
`VITE_WEBRTC_SIGNALING_URL`. To deploy it together with the encrypted sync
relay, and to measure the delay from where you are, see
[the share servers on Cloudflare](/sync/relay-server/) (`npm run owner:share`).

To run your own Node server with the same rules, start
`sync-server/collab-server.mjs` with `COLLAB_E2EE_ONLY=1`. Rooms unchanged
for `COLLAB_RETENTION_DAYS` days (90 by default) are deleted. **End session**
works there too, with the same check: the request carries the value derived
from the room password that the room's name commits to. The room is then
taken out of the server's backups as well. A backup the server cannot
rewrite at that moment (another program has it open, or the disk is full) is
kept as it was, and the room is taken out of it with the next backup round.

pages.title: Encrypted share link
pages.description: Share a read-only copy of one note as a link that carries the note itself, encrypted. No server, no account.
pages.md:
**Share as encrypted link** (command palette) turns the open note into a link. The note
is compressed and encrypted on your device and travels **inside the link**. Whoever opens
the link sees a read-only copy, decrypted in their own browser. Nothing is uploaded, and
neither of you needs an account.

## Why no server sees it

The link looks like this:

```text
https://lumen-md.vercel.app/#view=<encrypted note>&key=<key>
```

Everything after `#` is the *fragment*. Browsers never send it to a server: it is not
part of the request, and it is not in the `Referer` header. So the server that serves
Lumen gets a plain request for its home page, with no byte of the note or of the key.
The tests check this: `e2e/share-link.spec.ts` records every request the viewer makes,
its headers and its body included.

- **Encryption:** AES-GCM with a 256-bit key, made at random for each link (WebCrypto).
  If one character of the link changes, or the key is wrong, the note does not open. It
  never shows altered text.
- **Compression:** `deflate-raw` (CompressionStream) runs before encryption, so a typical
  note of 20 KB makes a link of about 7,000 to 11,000 characters.
- **Read-only:** the viewer shows the note. It does not save the note into the
  recipient's notes, but they can copy the Markdown or download it as `.md`.

## Options

- **Expires:** never, or after 1, 7 or 30 days. The date is inside the encrypted note,
  and the viewer refuses the note after it. This is a promise of the viewer, not of the
  cryptography: the link still holds the note, so someone who kept it could decode it by
  hand.
- **Send the key separately:** you get the link without its key, and the key on its
  own. Send them by two different routes (for example, an email and a message). Someone
  who opens the link without the key is asked to paste it.

## Large notes

A link holds at most 32,768 characters of encrypted data, so that it stays usable in
browsers and in messaging apps. For a larger note, the dialog offers an **encrypted
file** (`.lumenshare`) and a short link that holds only its key. The recipient opens the
link and picks the file. The file is decrypted on their device too.

Opening a link or a file inflates the note at most 100 times its compressed size,
so a crafted link can't freeze the viewer. Every note Lumen shares fits that bound.

## Which address the link opens

A link opens the viewer on a web address the recipient can reach. A link made in the
desktop or mobile app, or on `localhost`, names the public app,
`https://lumen-md.vercel.app` (a build can name another one with `VITE_SHARE_ORIGIN`).
A Lumen served over https from a public host keeps its own address.

## Who can read it

Anyone who has the whole link (or the file and its key link), and nobody else. Treat
the link like the note itself: don't post it where others can read it.

pages.title: Sharing, roles and comment threads
pages.description: Share a note to view, comment or edit with a link that expires; revoke it; comment threads with mentions.
pages.md:
With a [persistent collab server](/collab/webrtc/), a note in a
collaboration session can be shared with a **link that gives one role and
expires**. The server holds everyone to their role, also in end-to-end
encrypted rooms.

## Share a note

1. Start a collaboration session (⌘K → *Start collaboration*).
2. ⌘K → **Share this note…**.
3. Choose the access and the expiry, optionally who it is for, and press
   **Create link**. The link is copied.

| Access | Can |
|---|---|
| **Can view** | read the note and its comments, see who is there |
| **Can comment** | also write, answer and resolve comments |
| **Can edit** | also change the note |

Links expire after 1 hour, 1 day, 1 week or 30 days. The link contains the
room's key (so the note can be decrypted) and the link's id (what the server
checks). Send it only to the person it is for.

## Revoke a link

⌘K → **Share this note…** lists the note's links with their state. Press
**Revoke**: the server stops letting that link in at once and drops anyone
still connected with it **within a few seconds** (the server checks every
second). Their copy of the room key opens nothing without the server.

## Shared with me

⌘K → **Shared with me** lists the links you opened on this device, with
their access and whether they are still active, expired or revoked.

## Comment threads

Select text and add a comment (⌘K → *Add comment*). A comment stays on
its words while others edit around it, in Hebrew too. Write `@name` to
mention someone (also after a Hebrew prefix, as in `ו-@דנה`), answer in
the thread, and resolve it when done.

The threads are kept in the room and, for the note's owner and editors, in
a file next to the note: `plan.md` → `plan.comments.json`. It travels with
the vault (git, sync, export). When the note is shared again, its threads
come back and are placed on their quoted text.

## How it is enforced

- The first time you share a note, your device **claims the room** with an
  owner secret kept in its encrypted secret store; the server keeps only its
  hash. After that, only the owner gets editor access without a link.
- A room with share links is synced **through the server only**, not over
  the peer-to-peer WebRTC mesh, which could not hold anyone to a role.
- Each room has two documents on the server: the note and its comments.
  "Can view" may write neither, "Can comment" only the comments, "Can edit"
  both. A change sent by someone without the right is dropped, along with
  their connection.
- In the app, a view or comment link opens the note read-only and hides
  the comment controls a viewer can't use.
- Collab cursors and name labels follow the line's direction, so they sit
  on the right side of the caret in Hebrew and Arabic text, and a name in
  one script never reorders text in another.

## For server operators

`sync-server/collab-server.mjs` stores rooms' owners and share links in
its SQLite database (no document content). `COLLAB_REVOKE_CHECK_MS`
(default 1000) sets how often live connections of revoked or expired links
are dropped.

pages.title: Suggestions and named versions
pages.description: Suggest edits that change nothing until someone accepts them, accept or reject one person's suggestions at a time, see who wrote what (the AI included), and name versions to compare word by word.
pages.md:
## Suggesting, alone or together

Turn on **suggesting mode** (track changes) from the command palette. From
then on, what you type and delete is written as a suggestion, and the text
itself doesn't change until someone accepts it:

```md
The report is {++almost ++}{>>@Dana<<}done{--, finally--}{>>@Avi<<}.
```

This works in the source editor and in WYSIWYG, alone and in a shared note.
In a shared note, everyone sees each suggestion as it is made.

## Who suggested what

- Each author's suggestions are underlined in their own colour, and hovering
  shows the name.
- Suggestions the AI made carry the author **AI** and are marked "AI".
- The command palette lists everyone who has a suggestion in the note:
  **Accept all from Dana (3)** and **Reject all from Dana (3)**, and the same
  for each other author, the AI included. These resolve only that person's
  suggestions; everyone else's stay as they are.

## Named versions

In a shared note, open **Named versions…** from the command palette.

- Give the current text a name, such as "Before submission". The version is
  saved inside the shared note, so everyone in it sees the same list. Only
  editors can save a version.
- Pick any two versions, or a version and the current text, to compare them.
  The comparison is word by word: additions are green, removals are red, and
  you see how many words were added and removed.
- The comparison is built for Hebrew. A word keeps its one-letter prefixes
  (ו, ה, ב, ל, מ, ש, כ), its niqqud, and a geresh or gershayim inside it
  (צה״ל), so "הבית" changed to "ובית" shows as one changed word, not one
  changed letter.

## Tested

- Twenty Hebrew comparison cases, covering prefixes, niqqud, gershayim,
  numbers, punctuation and mixed Hebrew and English, are checked on every
  run.
- By-author accept and reject are tested to change only that author's
  suggestions.
- A two-browser test runs through the collaboration server. A participant
  suggests and the owner's text doesn't change. The owner accepts and the
  change lands. A version named by the owner then shows up for the
  participant, with the word-level comparison.

pages.title: Real-time WebRTC collaboration
pages.description: Multi-cursor editing over a peer-to-peer mesh — no server account, no central log of your doc.
pages.md:
Lumen ships a real-time collab mode powered by [Yjs](https://yjs.dev)
over WebRTC. Open a doc, share the room link, and every keystroke
syncs to every peer in <30 ms.

## Start a session

`⌘K → Start collaboration`. A toast confirms the room name + copies
the share link to your clipboard:

```
https://lumen.app/#room=lumen-bright-river-77
```

Anyone with the link enters the same Y.Doc. Their cursor + selection
appears in your editor, coloured by their auto-assigned chip.

## Awareness UI

Each peer publishes:

- **Display name** — random adjective+noun combo, e.g. "Marble".
- **Colour** — auto-picked HSL hue.
- **Cursor + selection** — re-published on every selection change.

The editor renders peer cursors with a small floating name tag above
the caret. A peer's selection highlights with a translucent version of
their colour. The list of active peers shows in the status bar.

## End-to-end encryption

Without a password, the room is **not** end-to-end encrypted. Peers sync
the plaintext Yjs document, so any signaling server that relays
messages, the persistent collab server and anyone with the room link can
read it.

Set `localStorage["lumen.collab.password"]` (or append `&password=…` to
the share link) to change that. The editor's document then stays
local, and only AES-GCM-256 ciphertext envelopes (key = PBKDF2 of the
password, salted with the room name) go to the mesh and to any
persistence server. Peers without the password receive only ciphertext
and see a "Can't decrypt this room" error.

The password also encrypts y-webrtc's signaling, so a peer without it
can't connect at all and relays never see presence (names, colours,
cursor positions) — only peers holding the password do. Metadata such
as the room name and the volume and timing of edits is still visible.
A wrong password therefore looks like an empty room: Lumen asks before
sharing your document into it rather than forking the room silently. See
[End-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/) for the full threat model.

## Rooms evaporate when the last peer leaves

WebRTC is peer-to-peer — there's no server holding the doc. The doc
state lives in each peer's Y.Doc, replicated over the mesh. Once
everyone leaves, the state is only in the OPFS workspace of whoever
saved it. To get persistent rooms (the Notion / Google Docs feel),
enable [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/).

## Comments / annotations

Inline comments anchor to text ranges via Yjs `RelativePosition`, so a
comment on "neural networks" stays attached to those words even when
collaborators insert paragraphs above. Open the comments panel from
`⌘K → View comments panel`.

## Performance budget

- Room cap: 20 simultaneous peers (raise via the WebRTC provider's
  `maxConns`).
- Per-update overhead in password rooms: ≈ 40 bytes (IV + GCM tag +
  envelope framing) per edit batch; edits made in the same tick share
  one envelope.
- Initial join: full Y.Doc snapshot synced via the signaling channel
  (≈ 1 KB per 1k characters of doc).

For documents larger than ~50k characters or sessions with >20 peers,
move to [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/) which uses
the persistent collab server (Hocuspocus + SQLite, `sync-server/collab-server.mjs`).
